"Commandant Rena Vasić. Six years commanding the Thornfeld Regional Police. During her tenure use-of-force incidents dropped by sixty percent. She testified against fellow officers twice. The police association called her difficult."
"Vasić is the reform candidate. She has done the thing she claims to believe in. That is rarer than you think."
"She will face resistance from the senior command. They will not follow her willingly. She knows this. She expects to fight an internal war for the first two years. She told me that herself."

Vasić's file includes a single disciplinary note: 'Refused a direct order to reassign an officer accused of excessive force. Requested investigation instead. Investigation confirmed the accusation.' She was suspended for three days. She returned to work on day four.
Vasić. Reform from within. The force needs to know the rules have changed.
Interesting. Let me hear about Šolc.
Tell me about Stańko.

"Dr. Mirko Šolc. Professor of Criminology at the University of Ashenmere. Authored the standard text on community policing. Has consulted for police forces in four countries. Has never served in one."

"A civilian commissioner is unprecedented. It is also exactly what the police force needs — someone who does not think like a police officer. The institution has spent twenty years protecting its own. An outsider is the only way to break that cycle."

"He will have no operational credibility with the rank and file. None. They will not follow him because he cannot command them — he has never done their job. If he orders a dispersal, will a sergeant with fifteen years of service listen? I do not know. Neither does he."

Šolc's published framework proposes a police force organized around community accountability boards, civilian review panels, and de-escalation training as standard practice. It has never been implemented at national scale.
Šolc. An outsider. Exactly what a system that protects its own needs.
Let me reconsider Vasić.
Tell me about Stańko.

"Deputy Commissioner Lev Stańko. Seventeen years in the force. Rose through the ranks without a single disciplinary note — which, in this force, either means he is exceptional or he is careful. He was not at Kravenstal."

"Stańko knows the force. He can manage it. He will not make enemies and he will not make dramatic changes. If you want stability — if you want the police to function while the investigation proceeds — he is the correct choice."

"Stańko is the continuity candidate. He worked under the Commissioner who ordered the surveillance programs. He said nothing. He filed no complaints. He is not responsible for what happened — but he also never stopped it. A man who does not make trouble in a troubled institution has made a choice."
Stańko's personnel file is clean. In a force where 'clean' sometimes means 'nobody looked,' this is either reassuring or suspicious.
Stańko. Stability. The investigation proceeds without institutional chaos.
Let me reconsider Vasić.
What about Šolc?

It takes you until two in the morning. Four pages. The keys are listed by building. The accounts are listed by number. The last paragraph is three sentences long and the second sentence is your father's name.
"Good."
✦Good. Well written. Honest. A Chancellor who can lose. He's said one word and meant three, and the third is the one he'll never say aloud: I hoped you'd write that one.
Four pages: every key and every account, and Father's name in the last paragraph. Sealed until Wednesday.
Two pages. The first concedes, cleanly. The second is a programme for the opposition benches: nine bills you'd table in the first month, starting with the one Kolvar has promised to repeal.
"Combative."
✦I lose an office, not an argument. Vyktor heard a threat in it. Kolvar will too, if he ever reads it. I'd rather be feared on the benches than forgotten in a library.
A concession with nine bills attached. If I lose, I'll be on the first bench by Friday.
Vyktor takes the empty folder without a word. At seven the next morning it's back on the desk with two pages in it, typed, in his voice, which is to say in a voice indistinguishable from yours.
"Done. In case."
✦Halvek never wrote one either. I used to think that was arrogance. Tonight it felt like fear, and I can't tell the two apart when they're mine.
I wouldn't write it. Vyktor did, in my voice, in case.

✦The matron stares at the check for a moment before she takes it. She does not thank me — she looks at me like she is revising something she had decided about politicians. The boiler is fixed by Thursday. Liora sends a note that says only: good. Two words. The highest praise she gives.
"Don't tell anyone you did it, Mum. The minute it's in the Herald it stops being a boiler and becomes a policy you never made."
₭1,500 from my own pocket. One boiler fixed, and a two-word note from Liora: good.

✦The state process takes eight weeks. The boiler is still broken when the funding clears. The matron has wrapped the children in extra blankets and moved them into the south wing, which gets afternoon sun. Liora stops calling for three weeks. When she does call, she doesn't mention the orphanage. That is worse.

The funding clears on the fifty-sixth day: ₭4,200 for the boiler and three months of coal. By then the matron has spent ₭140 of her own wages on blankets. Nobody reimburses her. There is no form for it.
The state paid, eight weeks late. The matron paid first, out of her own wages.

✦Liora doesn't follow me out. I wait by the car for four minutes before she appears. She gets in without speaking. We drive back to Ashenmere in silence. She is not angry — she is something quieter and harder to fix than angry. She has learned something about me today that she did not want to know.
"Do you know what the matron said after you left? 'They always look at the boiler. Then they look at their watch.'"
No cheque, no promise. The children stay in the south wing, and Liora stays quiet.
"Understood."

She closes the folder and squares it to the edge of the table. The reserve goes from ₭14 million to nothing. The Sevagrad garrison loses its winter fuel allocation; two companies are moved into the rail depot at Brask to sleep beside the locomotives for the heat.
"I don't resign over money, Chancellor. I resign over orders. This was money. Remember the difference when you give me the other kind."
✦Fourteen million from the border. Vostane exhales. Marić doesn't look at Dusek. Nobody thanks anyone. That is how you know a cabinet decision was real.
The coupon is paid, the widows are paid, and two companies sleep beside locomotives in Brask.
The tranche is 61,000 pensioners at ₭76 a month for three months: ₭13.9 million. Vostane rounds it up in her head and nods.
Marić takes an envelope from his inside pocket. He writes on it with the cabinet pencil, signs the back, and leaves the date line empty. He slides it across the table to you, not to Vyktor.

"My resignation. Undated. Keep it in your drawer. The day you have to put a date on it, I'll understand why. Until then I'll go and tell four thousand widows 'next quarter' in my own voice. They deserve that much."
✦He worked the Sarenka face for nine years before he ever wore a tie. He knows exactly what ₭76 buys in a pit town in winter. So do I.
Put the envelope in the drawer, undated. Next quarter, again.
"They'll pay it. Then they will put it on freight rates within the month. You will see it in Thornfeld bread by the spring: twelve percent on flour haulage. I'd like that minuted as well."

The levy decree goes out under seal at four. By six, three of the Aldenmoor houses have announced 'temporary rationalization of the Lytheiran route.' Eleven hundred dockers are told to come back in a fortnight.
✦Fourteen million from people who will barely notice it. The dockers noticed it by six o'clock. Money never leaves the top of the building without stepping on someone on the way down.
Fourteen million from the docks. Thornfeld pays some of it back in bread.
"Then I want it in writing, over your signature, because I will be the one on the telephone to Petravar on Friday morning."

Nine days later the Orythian rating houses cut Veltrian paper by two notches. The November auction clears at 11.2 percent instead of 7.8. On the Republic's existing paper, that difference is roughly ₭9 million a year, every year, until somebody earns the two notches back.
Vostane's note of dissent is three lines long and goes into the cabinet record unamended. She does not resign. She stops arriving early.
✦I saved fourteen million this quarter and bought a bill for nine million every year after. Nobody in Kravenstal will ever know I did that for them. Everyone in Petravar will remember it.
The widows are paid. The Republic now borrows at eleven percent.

The Orythian contract is signed in Petravar on the Monday. Twenty-four airframes, ₭4 million, delivery in nine days by ferry flight. The contract has a maintenance annex: forty Orythian technicians at Sevagrad field for five years, on Orythian salaries, answering to an Orythian major.
"The jets are the best thing we have ever owned. The annex is the most expensive thing we will ever sign. I want both of those in the minutes."
"Vukov will count them from the air on the first day. He will count the technicians on the second."
Twenty-four Orythian jets at Sevagrad, and forty Orythian technicians to keep them flying.

The tank contract goes to the Kravenstal works: ninety hulls over eighteen months, ₭2.5 million, eleven hundred jobs. The design is twelve years old. The steel is Veltrian. The night shift starts on Thursday.
"They will not beat a Tyvaren tank in the open. They will be there, and they will be ours, and nobody in Petravar can switch them off. That counts for something."
✦Eleven hundred jobs in Father's town, building machines that will lose a fair fight. I know which half of that sentence the Worker will print.
Ninety Kravenstal hulls over eighteen months, eleven hundred jobs, and a design twelve years old.

The Gravenmark line is surveyed in a week: eleven kilometres of concrete, anti-tank ditches and three observation posts on the high ground. ₭1.5 million. The engineers start at the north end. They will reach the south end in seven months, if it does not rain.
"Concrete is honest. It says exactly what we intend: we will not go to them, and they will pay to come to us. It also says we expect them."
"Cheap. Visible. Permanent."
Eleven kilometres of concrete, begun at the north end. Seven months, if it does not rain.
Dusek closes all three folders and stacks them in order, jets on top. She does not argue. She asks for the decision in writing, which she has never asked for before.
"When the border tests us, I will need to tell my officers why we are fighting with Halvek's rifles. I would like to quote you exactly."
✦The treasury keeps ₭1.5 to ₭4 million it does not have anyway. The army keeps a sentence of mine, in writing, for the day it needs someone to blame.
No procurement. Dusek has my decision in writing, for later.

✦The room goes very still. Brenner's glass is still raised. He holds it there for a moment, then drinks — slowly, watching me over the rim. The other officers follow. Nobody laughs. Vyktor exhales beside me. The cameras get the image: Chancellor and General, glasses raised, eyes level. What it looks like in the morning papers depends entirely on the caption.
"Even."
Obedience answered patience, glass for glass. The caption decides who won.

✦I laughed. Not a politician's laugh — a real one, short and dry. 'The General keeps us all humble,' I said. The room relaxed on cue. Brenner smiled. The cameras caught a pleasant evening at the Officers' Mess, which is exactly what Vyktor wanted and exactly what Brenner expected. He will try again with something that can't be laughed off.
"Postponed."
I laughed it off. Brenner smiled and filed the joke away for later.

✦The room went silent the way rooms go silent when something irreversible has just happened. Brenner set his glass down. He did not argue. He nodded once — the nod of a man who expected this, or wanted it — and walked out through the side door. Three generals followed him. Four stayed seated. Vyktor spent the rest of the evening working out which four and what it means.
"Four."
Brenner dismissed at his own toast. Three generals walked out with him. Four stayed.
"Good. Then I have bought the only thing I could never afford. Aleksei. Come and shake the Chancellor's hand."
Aleksei crosses the room. His handshake is dry and brief. He looks at you the way his father looked at the map of Veltria in your office: as something that will be his to manage soon.
"No better, no worse. I'll hold you to the first half, Chancellor. My father's friends will hold you to the second."
Stefan Morvec dies eleven days later, at 04:20, facing the harbor. Four thousand people line the road to Aldenmoor Cathedral. Half of them work for the house. The other half came to make sure.
✦I gave my word to the worst man I ever liked. Now it belongs to his son, who will spend it the way young men spend inheritances: all at once, and to prove something.
Stefan is buried. My word passes to Aleksei with the rest of the estate.
Stefan laughs until he coughs, and coughs until the nurse comes in, and waves her out again.
"There she is. I wondered when you'd arrive. Aleksei, the green boxes in the vault. All nine. Have them in the Chancellor's car before she leaves."
"Father. Those are the house."
"Those are the reasons people are afraid of the house. You will need to learn to be feared on your own, or not at all. Better you learn it now, while I'm here to watch."

Nine green document boxes ride back to Ashenmere in the boot of your car. Thirty-one years of payments: judges, ministers, two Archbishops' secretaries, a Lytheiran trade attaché, and a deputy in your own Interior Ministry who is still drawing a salary. Stefan Morvec dies nine days later. Aleksei does not attend the reading of the will. He has already read it.
✦Nine boxes. I own half the Halvek generation now, the way he did. I tell myself the boxes will stay closed. He told himself that too, the first year.
Nine green boxes in the Chancellery vault. Aleksei will never forgive the price.
"No. Of course not. If you had said yes, I would have known you were frightened of me, and I would have died disappointed."
Aleksei turns from the window at last.
"Then we understand each other, Chancellor. My father spent thirty years buying this family's safety. You've just told me it was never for sale. I'll find out what it costs another way."

Stefan Morvec dies thirteen days later. The funeral is private. The house issues one statement, signed by Aleksei, announcing that 'the family's commitments to the Republic will be reviewed in full.' Three Aldenmoor shipping contracts with the state are cancelled the same week.
✦I told a dying man the truth because it was the law. His son heard a declaration of war. Both of them were listening to the same sentence.
No promise at the bedside. Three state contracts cancelled by the son before the mourning ends.

✦I speak for eight minutes without notes. I don't remember afterward what I said — something about the border holding, something about the Republic knowing their names even when it seems like it doesn't. They applaud. One soldier in the back is crying and trying not to show it. The press pool gets everything. Vyktor calls it the best footage of the campaign. Dusek says nothing, which means she agrees.
"The one crying at the back is Private Halek. Nineteen. His brother died at the pass in week sixty-five. I'll make sure he gets a copy of the footage."
Eight minutes without notes. The best footage of the campaign, and Private Halek at the back.

✦I eat the rations. They are exactly as bad as described. I ask the soldier with the standing-meal his name. Tomás. From Thornfeld. His mother runs a bakery. He shows me a photograph she sent. I don't know what I expected from this visit, but it wasn't to spend forty minutes looking at photographs of other people's families. The press gets nothing usable. I don't care.
"Tomás's mother wrote to the Ministry this morning. She wants to know who the woman was who ate with her son. I told her."
Forty minutes with Tomás from Thornfeld and his mother's photographs. The press got nothing.

✦Dusek doesn't argue. We pull back to the perimeter fence. The soldiers watch from the hut windows. Word spreads in the way that word always spreads in small enclosed places — fast and accurately. The Chancellor came to the fence and didn't come in. I hear that it's what they say. I don't correct it.
The press pool photographs you at the fence. The Herald crops the soldiers out. The Kravenstal Worker crops you out.
I came to the fence and didn't go in. The soldiers will tell it that way for years.

"Austerity will stabilize the Kroner within a week. The markets will respond positively. But the workers will riot, and the reformists will call you Halvek with a skirt. You are saving the economy by sacrificing the people who elected you."

✦I cut the budget to the bone. Public sector wages frozen. Infrastructure projects halted. The markets are happy. The people are furious. I saved the Republic's bank account and lost its soul. Kolvar is already drafting his campaign speech: 'She starved you to save her bankers.' He might be right.
The Kroner holds. The cost is written in the streets.

"The printing presses are running. The reserves are temporarily stabilized. But inflation will hit within the month. Bread prices will double. Pensioners will starve. You bought time, Chancellor. Time is the most expensive thing in economics."

✦I printed money to fill a hole. The hole is still there—it's just deeper now. The Kroner will collapse eventually. But eventually is after the election. I am buying votes with inflation I won't live to see. That is not governance. That is a Ponzi scheme with a nation.
The reserves hold. For now.

"You just transferred your personal fortune to the national treasury. The press is calling it 'the Ashavel Sacrifice.' The reformists are weeping in the corridors. The markets are stabilizing. You saved the economy with your own money."

✦I emptied my accounts. The country is solvent because I gave it everything I had. The newspaper headline reads: 'Chancellor Bails Out Republic with Personal Wealth.' I am either the most selfless leader in Veltrian history or the most desperate politician in an election year. Both are true.
The Republic stands. My accounts are empty.
The factory floor in Kravenstal is hot, loud, and exactly where you need to be. The workers look at you with tired eyes—eyes that have seen promises broken by every government for thirty years.
"You delivered the safety reforms. You appointed Marić. You held the line during the strike. The workers know what you've done. Now they need to hear you say it."

You speak from the factory floor, not a stage. You talk about the ventilation fans that are now installed in every mine. You talk about the minimum wage index. You talk about the widows' pensions. The workers listen. Some of them even clap.
The workers are listening. On to the next province.
The town square in Thornfeld is packed with farmers and their families. The Archbishop's shadow looms large here—his sermons shape their votes more than any politician's speech.
"Thornfeld is tricky. The Church opposed your education reforms. The farmers are struggling with food prices. But they respect tradition, and they respect a Chancellor who shows up."

You speak from the steps of the Town Hall. You talk about the agricultural subsidies, the road to Gravenmark, the price stabilization program. You don't mention the Church. They notice that you didn't.
The south is listening. On to the next province.
The university auditorium in Ashenmere is the hardest crowd you'll face. Students, journalists, professors—the people who dissect your every word and publish the analysis in the morning papers.

"These are the people who elected you. They are also the people who will turn on you the fastest if you disappoint them. Give them substance, not slogans. They can smell a talking point from a mile away."

You speak from the lecture podium. You talk about the constitution, the civil rights reforms, the press freedom charter. You take unscripted questions—risky, but necessary. A law student asks about the BNI files. You answer honestly. The room respects honesty, even when it's uncomfortable.
The capital is listening. On to the next province.

You sign the Charter into law. Within weeks, the first wave of Promethean Scholars arrives in Ashenmere. Nuclear physicists from Morivask. Aeronautical engineers from Orythia. Civil architects from Lytheira. They bring their families, their research, and their brilliance.

"The Iron Covenant is furious. General Brenner is demanding background checks on every single one of them. But the labs are humming, the patents are filing, and the military R&D division just made a breakthrough in rocket propulsion that puts us five years ahead of Tyvaren."

✦I opened the gates to the world's best minds. They came. They are building things that shouldn't be possible for a nation our size. The security risk is real—Krel has already caught two of them passing notes to foreign handlers. But the ones who are loyal are giving us the future. The fire is lit. Let it burn.
The Promethean Scholars arrive. The fire is lit.
You implement the Charter, but with Krel as the gatekeeper. Every scientist must pass a rigorous security review before they are admitted. The process is slow and invasive, but it ensures loyalty.

"We lost half the candidates to the vetting process. They didn't want to be interrogated by Krel's men just to take a job. But the ones who passed are clean, loyal, and brilliant. The labs are secure."

✦I got the minds, but I lost the volume. The vetting scared away the risk-takers—the ones who often make the biggest breakthroughs. But the ones who stayed are trustworthy. A smaller fire, but a safer one.
The vetted scholars arrive. The fire is contained.

"You rejected the Charter. The foreign scientists went to Orythia instead. Our domestic universities are underfunded and understaffed. The brain drain continues—but now it's our own minds leaving for better pay abroad."

✦I said no to the foreign minds. The Iron Covenant is pleased. But our labs are empty, our patents are stagnant, and the Orythians just hired the nuclear physicist I could have had. Caution kept us safe. It also kept us small.
The Charter is shelved. The Republic stays small.
"As you wish. I'll tell them to go home."
He stands and buttons his coat. At the door he stops, the way old men stop at doors in this building, and doesn't turn round.
"Kolvar's people won't make you the same offer, Chancellor. They'll just do it. I hope you win by more than thirty-eight thousand."
✦So do I. I'll never know whether I needed them, and that's the point of refusing. If I win, I won. If I lose, I lost a fair count. Father would have settled for either.
Every box counted. The polls open at seven, and I'll sleep, or try to.
Krel nods once in return and leaves. He doesn't say goodnight. He never does when he's working.

At 23:58 you take a sheet of Chancellery paper, write the time on it, and fold it into the back of your diary. You don't know why. Perhaps so that somebody, one day, can know exactly when it happened.
✦Only the wax. Nobody touches a ballot. I'll win or I'll lose, and either way I'll never know whether I won. Halvek must have had nights like this one. I used to think he slept well.
The wax is Krel's problem now. The question of whether I won is mine, forever.

The Forum's mission chief answers on the fourth ring, in a hotel bar in Stellamere. By 02:00 nine observers are on the night train to Thornfeld. By seven, one is standing behind every returning officer in the three districts, watching the wax.
"You've told every newspaper in the West that you expected your own election to be rigged. Kolvar will call it an insult to Thornfeld. He'll be right. It's also the only lock I couldn't have picked."

✦Nine strangers at the count, to stop a man who works for me. If a seal is defective now, it's defective in front of witnesses. Locking my own door from the outside is the strangest thing I've done in office.
Nine observers on the night train. Every seal in Thornfeld watched, Krel's included.
He looks at you for a long time. Then he takes a fountain pen from his inside pocket and writes three lines on the back of the visitors' card in his wallet, signs it, and puts it on the desk.
"The greenhouse was too exposed, I told you once. So is this office, now. You've made it a room with windows. Someone else will build a room without them. Someone always does."

The quiet office is closed by decree at 23:55, five minutes before the campaign silence would have made it impossible. Its six remaining staff are transferred to the Archive in Ostrava Street with full pensions and orders not to discuss their previous work.

✦Two years of a second government in the basement, ended on the back of a visiting card. I built it the way Father's enemies built theirs, one necessary night at a time. I don't know if closing it makes me better. It makes me finished with it.
Krel's resignation on a visiting card. The quiet office closed five minutes before the silence.
VYKTOR REZNIK :

"Stefan Morvec. Seventy-four. Widower. His family has held land in this country since before it was a republic. Timber, grain, river transport, the northern rail concession. He is listed in official records as a retired estate manager. He is not a retired estate manager."
How powerful is he really?
Why is he inviting me?
VYKTOR REZNIK :
"We were always going. The question is what we say when we get there."
What do we say?
VYKTOR REZNIK :

"Two district judges. The chairman of the northern rail authority. The bishop of Aldenmoor. And us. He builds tables carefully, Stefan Morvec. Every person at that table is there to send a message to every other person at that table."
What message are we sending?

"Article 7. The judicial independence provisions. The draft creates a Constitutional Court with appointment authority that bypasses the Assembly entirely. A chancellor appoints, a review panel confirms, and the Assembly has sixty days to object with a supermajority."
"You're asking us to ratify a mechanism that concentrates judicial appointment power in the executive. We just came out of a government that concentrated everything in the executive."
"The review panel is independent. The sixty-day window gives the Assembly meaningful oversight."
"A supermajority threshold for a sixty-day window is not meaningful oversight. It's a procedural obstacle."
What would you propose instead?
The supermajority protects judicial independence from Assembly politics. That's the point.
Aldric — I need twenty minutes with you before the session opens.
"Sixty-seven delegates in firm support. Nineteen in firm opposition. Twenty-six in what I would call thoughtful uncertainty — they have real questions and they're engaging with the process honestly."
"The remaining delegates are waiting to see which way the room moves. They will vote with what appears to be winning."
"We need sixty-seven votes to pass. We have sixty-seven. We have no margin."
The twenty-six in thoughtful uncertainty — what are their actual questions?
What worries you most about today?
VYKTOR REZNIK :
"Sixty-seven firm. That's the threshold. One delegate changes his mind and we're at a special session. Two and the reform fails its first vote."
"Kolvar has been working the uncertain delegates for three weeks. I don't know what he's offering but some of them are listening."

"I want to tell you something before we walk in there. One of the delegates — Mirova, from Sevagrad — came to my office yesterday. She said someone approached her with money. She didn't take it. She came to me."
Who approached her? Did she get a name?
What do we do with that information?

"Two serious candidates. Elara Vostane — former Central Bank analyst. Precise. Apolitical. She sees the economy as a set of equations to be solved. She's usually right about the equations and usually wrong about the people who have to live inside them."

"Alternative: Petr Kolvar. Twelve years in the Assembly. Knows how budgets pass through committee. He's a party man — loyal to whoever is in charge, which currently means loyal to you. That will last exactly as long as you're in charge."
What's Vostane's position on the deficit?
Kolvar — whose man was he before he was mine?
Who do YOU want at Finance, Vyktor?
"Interior is the dangerous one. Whoever sits in that chair controls the BNI — or disbands it. Two candidates."

"Danika Oberlin. Civil rights advocate. Fifteen years documenting BNI abuses. She will push for dissolution on day one. She's principled. She's also relentless. You should know that about her before you put her in the room."
"Alternative: General Perov. Military intelligence background. He'd keep the BNI but restructure it under civilian oversight. He believes in the apparatus — he just thinks Halvek used it wrong."
If Oberlin dissolves the BNI, what happens to the agents?
Perov — can he be trusted not to become the next Halvek?
I've heard enough. I know what I want.

"Defense is straightforward. Colonel Irina Dusek. She's the only serious candidate. Decorated. Respected by the rank and file. No political ambitions — she finds politics distasteful, which is either her best quality or her worst depending on the week."
"The Tyvaren border is her priority. She's been writing reports about northern defense gaps for three years. Nobody read them. She'd like someone to start reading them."
How serious is the Tyvaren situation in her assessment?
I know what I need to know. Let me decide.

"Finance: Vostane or Kolvar. Interior: Oberlin or Perov. Labor: Marić or Vane — the unions will fight you if you pick the wrong one. Justice: Theron or Garachi — idealist versus institutionalist. Defense: Dusek or Brenner — professional soldier or Iron Covenant insider."
"The real decision is Finance and Interior. Everything else falls into place around those two."
Tell me more about the Finance candidates.
Tell me more about the Interior candidates.
I know these people. Let me decide.
"No. Your face will change and Vael will read it. He's been reading rooms for forty years."
"My face doesn't—"
"Your face changes. Slightly. When you know something you didn't know thirty seconds ago. I've watched it for eight months. Vael will have it in forty-five minutes."
A pause.
"After."
Go in.
Nine faces turn when you enter. Vael stands. The others follow a half-second later — following his lead, which tells you something about who runs this room even when no one is supposed to run it.
LUCAN VAEL :
"Chancellor. Thank you for coming."
He is shorter than you expected. Older. His handshake is exactly as firm as it needs to be — not more.

"I'll begin directly, as I promised I would. The nine of us represent approximately forty percent of Veltria's private investment capacity. We are not here to threaten you. We are here because the current policy uncertainty is costing all of us money and we would prefer to stop losing it."
"We would like to understand what this government actually intends to do."
I'll be equally direct. What specifically concerns you?
I appreciate the directness. The government's economic intentions are public. The question is what you're prepared to contribute.
Tell me more about the uncertainty you're experiencing.
"Financial. Substantial. Structured as a consulting arrangement for a family member — clean on paper. The kind of thing that's difficult to prosecute and easy to deny."
"Whether it was accepted is the part I'm still verifying."
Whether it was accepted. You sit with that.
Go in.

"Article 14 of the constitutional reform draft requires that all institutions receiving state education funding deliver a curriculum that meets national standards in mathematics, natural sciences, history, and civic education. The Church operates two hundred and fourteen schools. They receive thirty-one million Krone annually in state funding. Therefore Article 14 applies to them."

"The history curriculum is the point of contention. Our history curriculum covers the formation of the republic, the Halvek years, and the democratic transition. The Church's current history curriculum covers the same period differently."
"It covers it accurately."
"It covers it from a particular perspective. The national curriculum requires a different perspective to be included alongside."
What specifically does the Church's history curriculum say about the Halvek years?
Archbishop — your response to that framing?
"The curriculum as written presupposes certain conclusions about history. About the Church's role in history specifically."
"The curriculum presupposes evidence-based reasoning. That's different."
"Is it."
Not a question.
"Yes."
"Faith is not the absence of evidence. It is a different relationship to evidence. The curriculum does not acknowledge that distinction. Our teachers notice."
Are you saying science and faith can't coexist in the same classroom?
What would the Church accept? What does acceptable look like?

"Two hundred and fourteen Church schools. Sixty-seven thousand students. Thirty-one million Krone in annual state funding. The Church schools serve primarily rural areas and small towns — many of them are the only school within forty kilometers."
"That last point is relevant. If the Church withdraws from the funding agreement rather than adopt the curriculum, those students don't have an alternative government school to attend."
"I would not withdraw from the funding agreement. I want to be clear about that. But the situation you've described is accurate and you should understand it."
Archbishop — what specifically does the Church object to?
Aldric — given that context, is there room for adjustment?
You read it. All of it. Forty-seven pages. It takes twenty minutes. When you finish you close the folder and put it face down on the desk.

Three people you trusted. One person you still trust, whose file says things that make that trust complicated. Two people who are already dead. One person whose file was clearly fabricated — the handwriting changes three times in a two-page entry.
"There are eleven thousand more."
CHANCELLOR ASHAVEL :
"Eleven thousand files."
"Eleven thousand active surveillance files. Plus archives. The archives are larger."
How many agents are actively maintaining these files?
Some of these are fabricated. How many?
I've seen enough. Let's hear from the others.
You close the folder without reading it. Oberlin looks up for the first time.
"That's one way to do it."
CHANCELLOR ASHAVEL :
"If I read every name before I decide, I'll make a personal decision, not a political one. I need to make the political one first."
"That's a very clean way to think about a very unclean problem."
She says it without judgment. She says everything without judgment. That is somehow more unsettling than criticism.
Tell me the scope. How many files, how many agents.
Let's wait for Vyktor and Dusek.

"Eleven thousand active files. Journalists. Academics. Three members of the current National Assembly. A retired judge. Two priests. And approximately four hundred ordinary citizens whose only qualification for surveillance appears to be that someone in the apparatus wanted leverage over someone who knew them."

"The name you recognized on the first page has been under surveillance for six years. The file records fourteen private conversations, two of which took place in this building, during the previous administration."
CHANCELLOR ASHAVEL :
"In this building."
"The BNI had access to the Chancellor's residence. Possibly still does. That is one of the reasons I am already in your office."
They may still have access to this office?
Get Vyktor and Dusek here. Now.

"Lucan Vael. Sixty-one years old. Inherited the Vael-Kross Holdings from his father in 1948. Under his father it was a mining and transport company. Under Marcel it became something larger — infrastructure, energy, banking, media. The media acquisition was 1954. Six months after the gap in the BNI file."
"He has been careful. He never held public office. He never appeared in photographs with Halvek. There is no document that directly connects him to the old regime's more uncomfortable decisions."
"That absence of documentation is itself a kind of documentation."
The BNI file gap — 1951 to 1953. Do you know what's in those years?
He owns media. Which outlets?
What do you think he's actually proposing?

"Infrastructure and Kravenstal employment. My guess: he wants to propose a public-private partnership. Vael-Kross funds the Kravenstal modernization and the northern road network. The government provides the regulatory framework and the land access. He gets the contracts, the depreciation tax treatment, and the goodwill."
"On paper it addresses your budget problem. On paper the workers in Kravenstal get jobs. On paper it's a good deal."
"What's not on paper?"

"What Vael-Kross gets that isn't in the contract. Influence. Access. The quiet understanding that a government that depends on private infrastructure investment doesn't make decisions that threaten private infrastructure investment."
Is there a version of this deal we could take without giving him that access?
What does he fear from our government? What is he trying to buy protection from?
I want to hear it from him directly.
I won't meet with him. Send a formal response through proper channels.
"My instinct is that it's neither a trap nor a gift. It's a negotiation. He needs something from us and he has something we need. That's business."
"The question is whether we can negotiate with him without becoming the kind of government that negotiates with Lucan Vael. Those are different questions."
"What's the difference?"
"One is a transaction. The other is a relationship. Transactions can be completed. Relationships don't end when the contract does."
What do you think he's proposing?
I want to meet him and make my own judgment.

"Three possibilities. He doesn't want a paper trail because the proposal involves things that shouldn't be on paper. He doesn't want his competitors to know he's approaching the government. Or he wants to make the offer personal — man to man, or man to chancellor — because he thinks that changes the dynamic."
"All three could be true simultaneously."
"Which do you think it is?"
"I think he's afraid of the wealth tax. And I think he wants to make an offer that makes you not want to implement it."
That's useful. What's the proposal itself?
Then I definitely want to meet him.

You step through the curtain. The sound hits you like a wall — twenty thousand people, and then, as you reach the podium, silence. Complete silence. The kind that only happens when a crowd is holding its breath.
You look down at the speech. Then you look up at the faces. You begin.
CHANCELLOR ASHAVEL :

"Citizens of the Republic. I stand here not as a victor, but as a servant. The election is over. The campaign is over. What begins today is harder than either of those things — the work of governing a country that has been through too much, and still believes it can be something better."
A murmur through the crowd. Not applause — something quieter. Recognition.

"I know there are people in this square today who did not vote for me. I know there are people watching from home who are afraid of what this government might do. I am asking for your patience. Not your agreement — your patience. Judge us by what we actually do. Hold us to it. That is your right and I am asking you to use it."
To your left, Jonas is very still. He has heard you give a hundred speeches. His expression says this one is different.

"The Republic does not belong to any party. It does not belong to any faction, any family, any interest. It belongs to the person in Kravenstal who went to work at five this morning. It belongs to the student in Dravenhollow who is the first in her family to finish secondary school. It belongs to the old man in Thornfeld who remembers what this country was before it forgot itself. It belongs to all of you. I will not forget that. Thank you."
The applause begins slowly — then swells. Not the manufactured roar of a rally. Something more genuine. Twenty thousand people deciding, individually, that this might be real.
Take a moment. Look at the crowd. Remember this.
Look at Jonas. He's the reason any of this matters.
You step to the podium. The crowd falls quiet. You set aside the safe version of the speech without looking at it.
CHANCELLOR ASHAVEL :
"Citizens of the Republic. I am going to speak plainly today, because I think plain speaking is exactly what has been missing from this podium for twenty-three years."
Somewhere in the crowd, someone cheers. A single voice. Then others join.

"This government inherited a deficit of money and a deficit of trust. I will not pretend otherwise. The books have been managed dishonestly. Institutions that were meant to protect you were used against you. People in positions of public trust treated those positions as private property. That ends today. Not as a promise — as a fact."
In the front row, three Assembly members are not applauding. You notice them. You continue.

"Reform is not punishment. I want to be clear about that. We are not here to settle scores. We are here to build something that works — for everyone, including the people who are nervous about what comes next. A government that operates honestly does not threaten honest people. Remember that."
Vyktor, at the side of the stage, makes a small note. You have named the problem without naming names. It is a careful line to walk and you have walked it.

"The next four years will be difficult. I am not going to stand here and tell you they will not be. Change is difficult. Accountability is difficult. But the alternative — another decade of managed decline, of quiet corruption, of a country that stopped believing in itself — that is harder. We choose the difficult thing. Thank you."
The applause is loud and immediate. Half the square. Then more. The three Assembly members in the front row eventually join in — slowly, reluctantly, but they join.
Glance up at the silent balconies. Let them know you saw.
Stay focused on the crowd. This speech was for them.
You step to the podium. You do not look at any of the prepared speeches. You look at the crowd for a long moment — long enough that Vyktor, at the side of the stage, shifts his weight.
Then you begin. The words from 2am. The ones you were not sure you would actually say.
CHANCELLOR ASHAVEL :

"I almost gave you a different speech today. A safer one. My chief of staff prepared three versions. They were all good. They would all have served the moment. I am not going to give you any of them."
A ripple through the crowd. Curiosity. Attention sharpening.

"My father worked in the Kravenstal foundries for thirty-one years. He never once appeared on a list, attended a party meeting, or asked anything from the people who ran this country. He just worked. When he got sick, the state hospital had a six-month waiting list. He waited. He died on that list. That is not a political story. That is just what happened to an ordinary man in a country that forgot ordinary men existed."
Complete silence. Twenty thousand people and no sound at all.

"I am not here because I wanted power. I am here because I got tired of watching what happened to my father happen to other people's fathers. I am here because someone had to be. And if I fail — if this government fails — I want you to remember that I stood here today and told you exactly why I came. Hold me to it. Please."

The silence holds for three full seconds after you finish. Then it breaks — not into applause exactly, but into something louder and less organized. People shouting. People crying. Someone near the front is just saying yes, yes, yes.
Jonas has turned away. You know why. You give him a moment.
"That was not one of the three speeches."
"It was better than all of them."
Let yourself feel it. Just for a moment.
Stay composed. The work starts now.

"Tyvaren operates a modern air force — primarily Confederation-supplied equipment. Their northern wing has approximately sixty combat-capable aircraft within range of our border. We have forty-two, eight of which are in maintenance rotation."
"In a direct engagement, we are at a disadvantage. That is not the relevant calculation. The relevant calculation is whether they want an engagement or a concession."
VYKTOR REZNIK :
"The Confederation won't sanction direct military action against Veltria. Tyvaren knows this. So do we. Which means this is about something other than military advantage."
Then what is it about?
What are our response options?
PROF. ALDRIC THERON :

"Three things changed in the last thirty days. Your government was sworn in — Tyvaren watched the election and did not like the result. The Arcturian Commonwealth made an overture to Veltria that became public — Tyvaren read that as a signal you might move east. And the Morivask situation is deteriorating in ways that affect the northern trade routes Tyvaren depends on."
"They are anxious. Anxious powers do one of two things — they negotiate or they probe. This is a probe. They want to know what you'll do before they decide which path to take."
"What we do in the next seventy-two hours tells them everything they need to know about this government's spine."
Dusek — given that framing, what do you recommend?
What are our actual options?
"Stand down."
Silence. Vyktor looks up. Theron stops writing.
"We scramble interceptors, we have a provocation. We have a provocation, we have a response. We have a response, we have an escalation. I have seen where that road ends, Chancellor."
A pause. When she continues her voice is exactly the same.
"It ends in fields."
"File a formal protest through diplomatic channels. Demand an explanation. Make the record. But do not give them the incident they came here looking for."
She does not say where she has seen this before. She does not explain what she means by fields. She waits for orders.
I hear you. What does a diplomatic protest actually accomplish?
Standing down completely — doesn't that confirm their read that we won't respond?
Show me all the options.
PROF. ALDRIC THERON :

"1947. Tyvaren conducted similar airspace incursions during the transition between the provisional government and the first elected chancellor. That chancellor scrambled interceptors. Tyvaren protested to the Asturien Forum. The Forum censured Veltria for escalation. It was three years before the diplomatic relationship recovered."
"1952. Similar incursion. That chancellor filed a formal protest and requested bilateral talks. Tyvaren agreed to talks and the incursions stopped for four years."
"The historical record suggests the diplomatic response produces better outcomes. I offer this as data, not as a recommendation. The situation today has variables that 1947 and 1952 did not."
Dusek — same question to you. What do you recommend?
Show me the current options.

The Commissioner enters. Vyktor closes the door from outside. Whatever expression the Commissioner wore in the corridor is gone — replaced with the careful neutrality of someone who has decided exactly how much to say and in what order.
DANIKA OBERLIN :
"Chancellor. I came directly to you because I am not certain how far this goes inside the ministry. I want that on record before I say anything else."

"Three weeks ago my office began a routine audit of the personnel rotation records — officers who transferred from BNI liaison roles into regular police assignments in the last five years. Standard post-reform procedure. What we found is not standard."

"Eleven officers. Across four districts. All former BNI liaison roles. All still active. All reporting — not to their district commanders, not to my office, not to any official chain of command I can identify. Someone is still running them. Not the BNI. Not the police. Someone else."

✦Eleven officers. Active, organized, reporting to an unidentified handler. The BNI was dissolved — or is being reformed, depending on which Interior Minister I appointed. Either way, there should be no active informant network operating inside the police force outside official channels. The fact that there is one means either the dissolution was incomplete, or someone rebuilt it, or it was never actually part of the BNI in the first place. All three possibilities point somewhere I do not want to look.

"I have the eleven names. I have their districts. I do not have their handler. That is why I am here rather than resolving this through the ministry. If the handler is inside the ministry, bringing this through official channels tells the handler we know."
Who do you suspect is running them?
I don't need the suspects yet. I need to decide how we investigate this.
The Commissioner enters. Their eyes move to Vyktor, register his presence, return to you. A small recalculation — not retreat, adjustment.
DANIKA OBERLIN :
"Chancellor. This is — broader than I expected to share. But all right."

"Eleven officers across four districts. Former BNI liaison roles. Still active, still reporting outside official channels. Someone is running an informant network inside the police force that the police force does not know about."
"How long have they been active?"
"The earliest transfer I can trace is four years ago. Before your government. Before the last government. This network predates the most recent administration."

"Then it survived the transition deliberately. Someone made sure these officers were transferred into regular police assignments where they would be harder to identify. That requires either foreknowledge of the transition or preparation for it."

✦Vyktor said it before I did. This network was prepared for the transition. Someone knew the government would change and moved their assets into positions that would survive the change. That level of foresight means either Halvek prepared it as a failsafe, or someone outside the government ran it from the beginning. Both explanations are worse than I want to consider before noon.
Who had the foreknowledge and the capability to set this up?
We decide the investigation method first. Then the suspects.
The Commissioner enters and stops. Oberlin is already seated. The Commissioner looks at her for exactly one second — not hostility, something more complicated — and then sits.
DANIKA OBERLIN :
"Chancellor. I came to you because I was not certain the ministry should hear this first. I see you have made a different decision. All right."
"Eleven officers. Four districts. Former BNI liaison roles. Still active, still reporting outside official channels. Someone is running them. I do not know who."

"Minister Oberlin — I am telling you this because the Chancellor has decided you should know. I want you to know that I considered not telling you. Not because I suspect you. Because I do not yet know where the handler sits and I did not want to tell anyone inside the ministry until I did. That calculation may have been wrong. I hope it was wrong."

✦The Commissioner is being exceptionally precise about their own uncertainty. That precision is either integrity or performance. Oberlin's expression is giving me nothing — she is processing, not reacting, which is either professionalism or preparation. I brought Oberlin into this room. I need to decide quickly whether that was right.
Minister Oberlin — your reaction to this information is your answer. What do you want to do about it?
We decide the investigation method together. All three of us.
Marić straightens. For the first time since you walked in, the tension in his shoulders releases slightly.
"I will have the first implementation proposals ready by end of week. Fourteen thousand families in the industrial regions alone."
"I will prepare the legal framework. And the list of complications. There will be complications."

The table that has seen seventeen governments settles into a different kind of silence. Not the silence of an argument paused. The silence of people who have decided something and are beginning to understand what that means.
Let's get to work.
